activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wet mittens and boots are left out to dry after playing in the snow.
story:
Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. Snow! The backyard was all white.

"Snow day!" said Mom. Chloe put on her boots. She put on her mittens. They were red and fuzzy.

Chloe ran outside. The snow was cold and soft. She made a snowball. She patted and patted. Her mittens got very wet. Snow went into her boots too. Her socks felt squishy and cold.

"I want to slide!" said Chloe. She slid down the little hill. She laughed and laughed. Then her mittens dripped. Drip, drip, drip.

Mom called her inside for warm cocoa. Chloe pulled off her wet boots. "My mittens are all soggy," she said.

"Let's hang them up," said Mom. They hung the red mittens on a low hook. They set the boots by the door, toes out.

"I want to go back out," said Chloe. She touched her mittens. Still wet! She waited. She looked out the window. She sipped her cocoa.

At last she touched them again. Dry and warm! Chloe put them on. She wiggled her fingers. "My mittens are ready!" she shouted. And she ran back out to the snow.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Today is the day that is happening right now.
story:
Avery sat in her car seat. The seat belt clicked. "Mommy, is today library day?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Today is now. We are in the car now."

Avery looked out the window. A dog ran by. Now there was a dog. Now the dog was gone. "Where did it go?" she asked.

"It ran away. It will run more later," said Mom. "Later is after now."

Avery put her hand near her ear. She could hear the wheels. Hum, hum, hum. "The wheels make a sound," she said. "The car goes, and then the sound comes."

"That's right," said Mom. "The wheels do that."

Avery saw a thin bird on a wire. The bird was thin and small. "Yesterday we saw a bird too," said Avery.

"Yes, we did," said Mom. "Yesterday is all done. Today we will get books."

"Then tomorrow?" asked Avery.

"Tomorrow we can read them," said Mom.

The car stopped. The library was here, today, right now. Avery held Mom's hand. The doors opened by themselves. "The doors move!" said Avery. "How do they know?"

Mom smiled. "Let's go find out."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Nova went to the park today. Her mom held her hand. Nova saw a boy by the swing.

"I was here tomorrow!" the boy said. Then he stopped. He thought hard. "No. I was here yesterday. Today is now."

Nova looked at the swing. "Can I swing now?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "But later we will eat lunch. Then later we go home. Tomorrow we can come back."

Nova climbed on the swing. Mom pushed. Up, up went Nova. Down came the swing. Up again. Each push made the swing go higher. That was funny to Nova. She laughed and laughed.

A dog ran by with a bag in its mouth. The bag fell out. A biscuit fell on the grass. The dog stopped. Then it ate the biscuit.

"Mommy! The bag fell, and the biscuit fell too!" said Nova.

Mom kissed Nova's head. "That's right. And now it is lunch time."

Nova slid down from the swing. She held Mom's hand. "Yesterday I was little," said Nova. "Today I am big."

Mom smiled. "Yesterday was the day before today," said Mom. "But you are big now."

They walked to the picnic table. Later, Nova waved at the park. "Bye, park! See you tomorrow!"

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Used needles go into a special hard box so nobody gets poked.
story:
Elias sat on the big paper bed. The nurse came in with a small tray. On the wall there was a red box.

"What is that box for?" Elias asked.

"You will see," said the nurse. She cleaned his arm with a soft cotton ball.

The nurse held up a tiny needle. Elias took a big breath. The needle went in, quick as that. "All done," said the nurse.

Then the nurse dropped the used needle into the red box. It went click, into the hard box and shut.

"Does the needle come back out?" Elias asked.

"No," said the nurse. "It stays in there. The box is hard so nobody gets poked."

Elias looked at the red box. So that is what it was for. The needle went in and stayed in.

Then Dad picked him up. "Ice cream time," said Dad.

At the ice cream shop, Elias got a small cone with pink strawberry. He held it with his good arm. "Look, Dad," he said. He pointed at the trash can. "My napkin goes in there and stays there too."

"That's right," said Dad. He took a big bite and began to smile.

Elias licked his cone. "Can I push the trash lever?"

"You can push it," said Dad. Elias pushed the lever with one finger. The napkin dropped down, and the little door swung shut.

"Bye bye, napkin," said Elias.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries.
story:
Raphael was at Grandma's house. He was painting a big sun. The sun was yellow and round. Grandma gave him red paint too. He painted a red bird next to the sun.

"I want to show Dad!" said Raphael. Dad was in the kitchen. Raphael ran to get him. He touched the sun with his finger. Oh no! The yellow smeared. The sun had a big smudge now.

Raphael looked at his finger. The paint felt squishy and wet. "The paint is still wet," he said. Grandma nodded. "Let's put it in the sun by the window," she said. Raphael set the paper down carefully. He did not touch it.

They ate apple slices and waited. Raphael peeked at the painting. He poked the sun very softly. The paint felt dry now. It did not smear! "Dad, come see!" Raphael called. Dad came in and smiled. "A red bird and a big sun," said Dad. "I love it!" Raphael hugged his paper. "Thank you, Grandma," he said. "Can we paint one more?"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Fans often wear their team's colors to show which team they cheer for.
story:
Anthony ran into the restaurant with his papa. A big screen glowed on the wall. Everyone was loud and happy. "The big game starts soon," said Papa.

Anthony looked around. Everyone wore green shirts. Green hats too. Green cups! Anthony looked down at his own shirt. His shirt was red. He felt sad. "Papa, I want green," he said.

Papa smiled. He sent Uncle Ben to the car. Uncle Ben came back fast. He held up a small green shirt. "This is yours," he said. Papa helped Anthony put it on. Now Anthony was green like everyone else!

A man at the next table pointed at Anthony. "You cheer for our team too," he said. Anthony nodded big. The game began. The crowd made a happy noise. Anthony clapped and clapped. The team ran fast on the big screen. Anthony jumped up. "Go, go, go!" he yelled. All the green shirts cheered with him. Anthony waved his arms high. The server brought a big plate of fries. Papa gave Anthony a fry. Anthony pointed at the screen and shouted, "We are winning!"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: One thing can belong to more than one group, like an apple is a food and also a fruit.
story:
Willow's class had a big job. They had to sort the play market. "Put the fruits on this shelf," said Miss Pam. "Put the foods on that shelf."

Willow picked up a red apple. She put it with the fruits. Ben pulled it back. "It is a food," he said. "I eat it at lunch." Willow pulled it too. "It is a fruit," she said. "It grows on a tree."

The apple went back and forth. Then it fell and rolled under the table. Willow got down on her knees. She reached far. She pulled the apple out.

"Watch," said Miss Pam. She put the apple on a small box. The box sat between both shelves. "Now it is with the fruits and the foods at the same time."

Willow clapped her hands. "One apple, two groups!" said Ben.

Willow ran to get more things for the box. A banana went in. A little cheese went on the food side. Her toy bunny stayed with the toys, and the soft duck too.

At play time, Willow told her mom all about it. "My apple had two homes," she said. "I learned a thing at school today." She held up her snack. "Same apple. Still yummy."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Stopping before the cup is full to the top makes it easier to carry without spilling.
story:
Sofia wanted to make her own breakfast. Mama put warm toast on a low plate. Sofia held the butter knife with the flat side down. She pushed the soft butter across the toast. The butter left little yellow trails. "Look, Mama! My toast has yellow roads on it." The bread got shiny and wet where the butter went.

Next came the milk. Sofia set her cup on the table. She poured and poured. The milk went up and up. It stopped right at the top edge of the cup. "Full to the top!" she said. Sofia picked up the cup. She took one step. The milk wobbled. Then a white wave slid over the edge and onto her toes. Milk made a puddle on the floor.

Mama gave her a towel. Sofia wiped her toes. Was the cup too full? She looked at the milk, then at the puddle. Maybe she could try again. Sofia poured a new cup. This time she stopped pouring before the cup was full to the top. She left some room up there. She walked across the kitchen. The milk wobbled a little bit. But it stayed inside the cup. Not one drop fell.

Sofia took a bite of her buttery toast. The butter tasted real and creamy. She paid attention to the cup as she drank. "Mama, I can carry it all by myself now. Want to see me do it again?"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow melts into water when it is brought inside where it is warm.
story:
Anthony woke up and jumped out of bed. The window was full of white. "Snow!" he shouted. "No school today!"

Mom smiled. "It is a snow day," she said. "A surprise snow day."

Anthony ran outside in his red boots. He made a big snowball. It was round and cold. He loved it so much.

"I will keep you forever," Anthony said. He put the snowball in his red bucket. He carried it to his room. He set it on the rug. "Sit there, snowball. One snowball, my best snowball."

Then Anthony went to draw. He drew a dark blue sky. He drew one sun. He drew two trees.

After lunch, he ran back to his room. "Hello, snowball!" he said.

But the bucket was empty. The snowball was gone! There was only a puddle on the rug. Water, water, and more water.

"Oh no," said Anthony. "My snowball ran away."

Mom came in. She looked at the puddle. She looked at Anthony. "Do you want to try again?" she asked.

Anthony got a new snowball from outside. He put it on the big table in the warm kitchen. He sat down. He watched it. He did not look away.

Drip. Drip. Drip. The snowball got small. Then it got smaller. Then it was a puddle too.

"So that is where you go," Anthony said. He carried the puddle outside in his bucket. He poured it on the snow. "Goodbye, water. Come back as snow."

Then he jumped in a big pile with both boots, one, two, and Mom said, "You are my little snowman now!"

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: In a drawing app, moving your finger across the screen draws a line.
story:
Myles went to Mama's office. He saw a tablet on her desk. "Can I draw?" he asked. Mama turned it on for him. The screen lit up bright.

Myles tapped the screen. He slid his finger across it. A blue line followed his finger! He slid again. Another line came. Myles laughed. He made a big squiggle. "It looks like a snake," he said. He added two dots for eyes. "Hello, snake," he whispered. Mama looked over and smiled.

Soon Myles was tired of drawing. "All done," he said. He pressed the button the way Mama showed him. The screen went dark. He folded his arms over the tablet to carry it. He set it in the drawer, nice and flat. "Bye, snake," he said. Then he waved at the window, and a bus went by on the street below.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: If you hold a book upside down, the words and pictures look upside down too.
story:
Matteo wanted to read his book. It was bedtime. He sat on the big bed next to Dad.

He opened the book. But the dog looked funny. The dog's feet were up. His ears hung down. Matteo laughed. "Silly dog!"

Matteo looked at the book. Then he looked at Dad's book. Dad's book was the other way. The words on Dad's page sat flat and neat.

Matteo had a problem. He turned his book around. Pop, the dog was right side up! The dog's ears stood up. His tail wagged in the picture.

"Dad, I fixed it!" said Matteo. Dad smiled. Matteo turned one page. Then he turned the next page. He saw the cat. Then he saw the bird.

Mom came in with a fresh blanket. It was soft and warm. "My turn," she said. She sat down too. Matteo leaned on her arm and looked at the pictures, all standing up the right way.

"Read to the end," said Matteo. Mom started at the front. Matteo pointed at the words. "That says dog," he said.

"Yes," said Mom. "Those letters say dog."

Matteo looked at the letters. He looked at the dog. The letters and the dog went together. He turned the last page. "The moon," said Matteo. "Goodnight, moon."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In basketball, players score by throwing the ball through a hoop.
story:
Rose sat high in the big stadium. Her mom and dad sat beside her. Her friend Ben sat next to her too. The crowd was loud, like a storm of voices. Rose held her spotted ball, a gift from her grandpa.

Below, the players ran fast. One player threw the ball up. It went right through the hoop. The crowd cheered and cheered. "I want to do that," Rose said.

After the game, Dad took her to a small court. There was a hoop, just her size. Rose planted her feet on the floor. She threw her spotted ball up. It missed. She threw again. The ball went through the hoop. It dropped down, down, down. Ben clapped his hands. "You did it, Rose!"

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: You can make a new friend by telling someone your name and asking theirs.
story:
Max got on the school bus. It was his first day of school. He found a seat by the window. The bus went bump, bump, bump.

A boy sat down next to Max. The boy looked at his shoes. He did not say a word. Max wanted a friend. He thought and thought.

"My name is Max," said Max. "What is your name?" The boy looked up. "I am Sam," he said. Then Sam smiled a big smile. "Want to see my sweet toy car?" asked Sam. "Yes!" said Max.

The bus stopped at school. Max and Sam jumped off together. They ran to the playground, side by side. "Let's play," said Sam. "Okay, friend," said Max.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A child's age is said with a number word, like 'I am four.'
story:
Sienna went to the store with Mama. "Let's buy apples," said Mama. Sienna put apples in the bag. "One, two, three," said Sienna. Mama added more. "Four, five," said Sienna. At the deli, a man was slicing cheese. "Six, seven, eight," the man counted out loud. Sienna waited and watched. Waiting was nice here.

Then a song played on the speaker. "Nine, ten," sang the song. Sienna liked that song. She did a little dance by the cart. Mama smiled.

At the checkout, a man said, "Hello! How old are you?" Sienna held up three fingers. The man waited. He looked at her fingers. Then Sienna said, "I am three!"

"You get a sticker," said the man. He put a shiny star on her hand. Sienna held up her fingers again. "I am three," she said. "I am three!" Mama laughed and pushed the cart to the car.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Snow melts into water when you bring it inside where it is warm.
story:
Logan looked out the big window. Snow was falling. White flakes danced down, down, down.

"Snowy day!" said Logan. He pulled on his warm coat. He put on his red mittens. Mama helped with his boots. Outside, the wind blew. It was windy too! Logan's hat almost flew away. He grabbed it and laughed.

Logan made a snowball. It was round and cold. He wanted to keep it. He hid it in his pocket. "I will show Daddy later," he said.

Inside, the house was warm. Logan took off his wet boots. He forgot about his pocket. Then he heard it. Drip. Drip. Drip.

There was water on the floor! Logan looked in his pocket. His snowball was gone. There was only a little puddle. "Oh no!" said Logan. The snow had melted. Warm house, melted snow.

Logan got a towel and wiped the water up. Then he ran to Daddy. "Daddy! Come see!"

They opened the door together. Brrr, the cold air rushed in. "Let's make a new snowball," said Logan. "A big one!" Daddy put on his scarf. Logan grabbed his mittens. Out they went, into the white, white snow.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut.
story:
Gabriel ran to the playground. He ran fast. The big kids ran fast too. The little kids went slow.

Gabriel wanted his water bottle. It was in Mom's bag. Mom opened the bag. Gabriel drank. Then Mom closed the bag.

"Look," said Mom. She pointed to the water fountain. Gabriel pressed the handle. The water went up. He let go. The water stopped. Open made it splash. Closed made it quiet.

Gabriel tried it again and again. Open, splash, splash. Closed, quiet and still.

"Hot day," said Mom. She gave him a cold juice box from the cooler. Gabriel held it. Cold felt good.

Then Mom spilled some water on the bench. She wiped it with a towel. Gabriel helped. Big wipe, small wipe.

At home, Gabriel opened the fridge. He got his apple. But he left the door open.

"Gabriel," said Mom. "Is it open or closed?"

Gabriel looked. He pushed the door. "Closed!" he said. He grinned. "Open. Closed. I can do both!"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In soccer, a team scores by getting the ball into the other team's goal.
story:
Juliette was at the big pool. Her swim team had a game day. Coach Sam gave them a soft ball. There were two little nets in the grass by the pool. "Kick the ball into the net," said Coach Sam. "That is how we score."

Juliette ran to the ball. She gave it a big kick. The ball rolled away. It rolled to the wrong net! Her friend Milo waved his arms. "Not that one, Juliette! That one is the other team's net!"

Juliette looked at the ball. Then she looked at the tall coach. She ran around the ball. She turned herself the other way. She kicked again. The ball rolled and rolled. It went right into the other team's net. "Goal!" shouted Milo. The team jumped up and down.

After the game, they all sat by the pool. Juliette put her toes in the cool water. "Same time next week," said Coach Sam. Juliette smiled and kicked her feet. "I can kick the ball to the right net now," she said. Milo laughed and splashed his toes next to hers.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Hanging your coat on a hook keeps it off the floor.
story: Brooklyn waited at the bus stop with her dad. Her coat lay on the ground by her feet. The wind blew. Her coat slid away down the sidewalk. "My coat!" said Brooklyn. Dad picked it up. He hung it on the little hook by the bench. The coat stayed right there. It did not touch the ground. Brooklyn hung her hat there too. One, two, three, she counted the hooks. Then Brooklyn tried to zip her coat all by herself. The zipper went up. Then it stopped. She tried again. Up, up, up it went. "I did it!" said Brooklyn. Dad said, "We can dream of carrots on the bus." Brooklyn patted her furry pocket. The bus came around the corner. Brooklyn picked up her coat from the hook and held it tight. "Zipped and ready," she said.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much.
story:
Audrey had been sick with a cold. Today Mom said, "Let's go to the pharmacy." Audrey held Mom's hand in the store. The floor was slippery, so she walked slowly. The pharmacist gave Mom some medicine. It was in a small white box.

At home, Audrey still felt tired. Mom made her favorite soup. Audrey took one bite. Then she took another. "I only want a little," she said. Mom smiled. "That's okay. When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much. Your tummy will want more soon."

After dinner, they called Grandma on the phone. Audrey ate a triangle of toast while they talked. She nibbled it, bit by bit. The next morning, Audrey's tummy made a big growl. "I'm hungry!" she said. Mom laughed and hugged her tight.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: When a birthday cake has candles, a grown-up is the one who lights them.
story:
Mia was four today. She wore her party dress to the park. The sky was cloudy, but that was okay. Grandma had a big cake. It had four little candles.

Mia grabbed a match box from the picnic basket. "I will light them!" she said.

Dad took the box gently. "Lighting is a grown-up job," he said. "You get the wish."

Dad lit the candles one by one. The flames stood up tall. Mia made a wish, big and quiet. Then she blew hard. All four flames went out. The smoke curled up like little ribbons.

Everyone clapped. Sam, the small twin, rubbed his eyes. He needed a nap. Mom locked the cake safely in the cooler so the ants would not find it. Then Dad handed Mia the first big slice. "Happy birthday, Mia," he said.

"Make a wish too, Daddy," said Mia.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
story:
Dylan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse said, "Time for your checkup, Dylan!"

Dylan jumped up. "Can I get a sticker after?" he asked.

"Yes," said the nurse. "First we look at your hands."

She held his hands up. Dylan saw little black dots on them. Dirt! He had played in the sand outside.

"Want to see something fun?" asked the nurse. "Come with me."

They went to the little sink. The nurse put soap on Dylan's hands. "Now we rub," she said. "We can sing while we rub."

They sang a happy song. They rubbed and rubbed. Bubbles grew big and white.

Then the water washed the bubbles away. Dylan looked at his hands. The black dots were gone!

"Where did the dirt go?" Dylan asked.

"Down the drain," said the nurse. "All gone."

Dylan smiled so big. His hands were clean and pink.

"Now you are ready for snack time," said the nurse. She put two crackers in his hand.

Dylan looked at his crackers. Then he looked at his hands. Clean hands, then crackers. He clapped and said, "Clean hands first!"

The nurse laughed. "Here is your sticker," she said.

Dylan stuck it right on his shirt and ran to show Mom.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
It was a rainy day. Asher went to the store with his dad. The store sold crayons in a big box.

Asher saw a red crayon. He saw a yellow one too. He picked up a green crayon. "Green like grass," he said.

Then he held two crayons. One looked like the sky. One looked like the night. "This one is not blue," said a girl next to him. "It is too dark."

Asher put the two crayons side by side on the floor. He found more blues in the box. He lined them up. The first was light, like the sky. The last was dark, like night.

"They are all blue," said the girl.

"Light blue and dark blue," said Asher. Dad smiled and picked him up. "Let's get the box with all the blues," said Dad.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Romy wanted her teddy. He sat up on the big shelf. She was too small to reach.

"I want Bear," said Romy. She stomped her foot. She felt mad.

Dad came in. "I can help," he said. Dad lifted Bear down. Now Bear was down low with Romy.

"Let's play slide," said Dad. "I will teach you a game." The little slide stood by the wall. Romy put Bear at the bottom. Then she carried him up, up, up the steps. She set him down at the top. Bear went down, down, down. Fast!

The small toy mouse went up too. He came down slow. Romy laughed. "Bear is fast. Mouse is slow."

Mom came in with a drink. "This cocoa is hot," she said. "Here is cold juice for you." Romy drank the cold juice. It was good.

Romy made a sign with Dad. It had a big arrow. The arrow pointed up the steps. She taped it on the slide.

Then something came down the slide. It was not Bear. It was the puppy! The puppy slid down and landed on a soft pillow.

"Again," said Romy. Up went the puppy, and down he came.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Library books are shared with many other people, so we take care not to tear or write in them.
story:
Naomi stood in the reading corner. Today she would get her very first library card. It was new and shiny, with her name on it.

"Pick any book you like," said Miss Ana, the librarian.

Naomi picked a book about a red bird. She sat down on a soft cushion. She opened the book to the first page. In her pocket, she had a fat blue crayon. She loved to draw circles. She pulled out the crayon. She held it near the page.

Then she saw the page. It had a small fold on the corner. Another child had read this book before her. Another child would read it after her, too. The book was for everyone to share.

Naomi put the crayon back in her pocket. "Can I have some paper?" she asked Miss Ana.

Miss Ana gave her a big white sheet. Naomi drew circle after circle. She drew a red bird in a circle too.

At the desk, Miss Ana scanned the book. "It is yours for now," she said. "Bring it back soon."

Naomi hugged the book and her paper. "I will take good care of it," she said.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
story:
Layla wanted to help Mom make bread. Mom gave her a bowl. It was heavy, but Layla held it with two hands.

Layla poured in the flour. White dust went up, up, up. She saw it float in the sun. She heard the spoon go tap, tap, tap on the bowl. The dough felt soft and squishy under her fingers.

Then Mom said, "Smell this. The bread is baking." Layla sniffed with her nose. "Mmm," she said. "I smell it with my nose."

After that, Mom held up a little mirror. Layla looked at her own face. She saw her nose had two little holes. She sniffed again. Both holes pulled the smell in.

"What are those called?" Layla asked.

"Nostrils," said Mom. "Your nose has two."

Layla sniffed once more. Then she waited by the oven, watching the bread get big.

At last Mom cut a warm slice. "A gift for my helper," she said. Layla took a bite. "I taste it with my tongue!" she said, and she jumped up and down.

Mom laughed and took another slice too.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A week has seven days.
story:
Paisley sat in her car seat. Today they were driving to Grandma's house. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "We will get there later."

Paisley looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. The cow mooed. Paisley laughed. Then the cow was gone. The car had moved past it.

"Grandma has a wild cat," said Mama. "And tomorrow we will look for eggs in her hen house." "What is tomorrow?" asked Paisley. "Tomorrow comes after today," said Mama. "Yesterday we packed your bag. Today we drive. Tomorrow we find eggs."

Paisley held up one hand. She counted her fingers. "Yesterday, today, tomorrow," she said. One, two, three. Then four, five. Then her fingers ran out. "Mama! My hand is too small!"

Mama laughed. "A week is seven days. You need more fingers." Paisley looked at her other hand. She counted on. Six, seven. All done!

The car stopped. "We are here now!" said Mama. Paisley looked out the window. Grandma stood by the door. Beside Grandma sat a wild cat, and on the cat's head sat one small egg. "Look, Mama!" said Paisley. "The cat found the first egg!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: A game has rules that all the players follow.
story:
Audrey was in the playroom with her brother Tom. They were playing the picture game. Mom sat on the soft rug nearby. The game had four red cards and one gold star. "The star goes to the winner," Tom said.

They took turns. Tom went first. Then Audrey went. "One turn for you, one turn for me," they said together. Audrey picked a card. It had a slow turtle on it. Tom picked a card. It had a fast bunny. Tom laughed and laughed.

Then Tom put the star in his own pocket. "I made a new rule," he said. "The star is mine now." Audrey stopped playing. She put her cards down. Tom waited, but no one played with him. The game was very quiet.

Tom took the star out of his pocket. He put it back on the rug. "Let's use the real rules," he said. Audrey smiled. They played again. One turn, then one turn. They said each card's name out loud. "Turtle!" "Bunny!" "Fish!" Audrey even got to spill nothing at all, because Mom brought two cups of juice with careful hands.

At the end, Tom won the game. But Tom gave the star to Audrey for one minute. Then Audrey gave it back. Mom clapped her hands. "Time for a snack," she said. Audrey held Tom's hand all the way to the kitchen.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: While you wait for a turn, you can play with something else.
story:
Charlie ran to soccer practice. He saw the big orange ball. It had a white star on it. Charlie wanted to kick it first.

But Maya got to the ball first. "My turn," she said. Charlie reached out his hand. He wanted to grab it. Then he stopped. Coach Ben blew his whistle. "Maya kicks first," he said.

Charlie stood still. Waiting felt very long. His feet wanted to wiggle. Then he saw the cones nearby. They looked like little hats. Charlie picked up three cones. He stacked them up tall. He put one small ball on top. It looked like a friendly snowman.

"Charlie, your turn!" said Coach Ben. Charlie looked up. His tower was done. Maya sent the orange ball rolling to him. Charlie kicked it far. "Nice kick!" Maya said. "Your snowman is silly," she said, and laughed. Charlie laughed too. "Next time I will build a dog," he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was empty. She wanted the yellow pudding in the fridge.

"Is it pudding time now?" she asked.

"Not now," said Mom. "Pudding is for later. Eat your soup first."

Iris puffed her cheeks. She was a little mad. She scratched the table with her spoon. Scratch, scratch, scratch.

Mom pointed at the clock on the kitchen door. "Look at the clock," she said. "The clock shows what time it is. When the big hand goes all the way around, it will be later."

Iris watched the clock. Tick, tick, tick. She ate one spoon of soup. She looked up. The big hand moved a little. She ate another spoon. Tick, tick, tick. The big hand moved some more.

"Yesterday I had pudding," said Iris. "Today I have soup first. Then pudding later!"

"That's right," said Mom.

The big hand went all the way around. Mom set the yellow pudding down. Iris clapped her hands.

"Now is pudding time!" she said.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: It is polite to wait until someone finishes talking before you start to speak.
story:
Milo had big news. His tooth was loose. He wanted to tell Grandma right away.

Grandma was on the phone. She was talking to Aunt Jo.

"Grandma! Grandma!" said Milo.

Grandma held up one finger. She kept talking. Milo tapped his tooth. He waited. It felt long.

Grandma said, "Goodbye, Jo." She put the phone down. Then she looked at Milo.

"Now I can listen," she said.

"My tooth is loose!" said Milo. "Look!"

Grandma looked. She smiled a big smile. "May I touch it?" she asked.

"Please do," said Milo.

Grandma touched it, soft and slow. "It will fall out soon," she said.

"Thank you," said Milo.

At bedtime, Milo sat on his bed. He licked his tooth, shiny and wet.

Tomorrow he would tell Dad. Dad would talk first. Then Milo would wait. Then Milo would talk.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
story:
James sat at the big art table. He was making a card for Grandma. He wanted to paint her favorite flower. The flower was pink. James looked in his paint cups. He had red. He had blue. He had yellow. He had green. He had white. But there was no pink. James frowned at his paper.

He tried the red paint first. He made a red flower. "Too dark," said James. He wanted pink. He tapped his brush and thought. He waited a long time. Then he looked at the white cup. He put his brush in the white. He stirred it into the red paint. Round and round the brush went. Slowly, the red turned pink. Soft, light pink!

James painted a new flower. It was pink, just like Grandma's favorite. Then he painted green leaves beside it. Then he painted a blue pond below it, and a yellow sun up high. Miss Amy leaned over his table. "What a pretty flower," she said. "How did you get that color?"

James held up his red cup. Inside, one last bit of pink was hiding at the bottom. He smiled. "I found it," he said.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Pouring slowly helps keep milk from splashing out of the cup.
story:
Lily stood in the big restaurant kitchen. The cook, Mia, had made warm toast. "You can help," Mia said. Lily wanted to spread the butter all by herself.

Lily took the little knife. Mia held the toast steady. Lily pushed the butter. It slid across the toast. "I did it!" said Lily.

"Now the milk," said Mia. She set a cup on the low table. There was a map of the kitchen on the wall, up high. Lily looked at the cup. She poured fast. Milk splashed out! It ran onto the table.

"Oh no," said Lily. Mia wiped the table. "Try again," she said. Lily picked up the jug. This time she poured slowly. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop came out.

"Look, Mia!" said Lily. Mia smiled. "That will be a good cup of milk," she said. Lily carried it to the table, step by step.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A new pet may hide at first while it gets used to its new home.
story:
Ella went to the pet store with Dad. She held a little bag of cat food. The store had a bell that would ring when the door opened. Ring, ring, it went.

Ella looked at all the pets. She saw a small gray kitten. "This one," she said. Dad put the kitten in a soft carrier. The carrier had a strong handle. Ella helped carry it to the car.

At home, Ella set out a bowl of food. But the kitten ran under the bed. Ella could not see it at all. "Where did it go?" she asked. She sat down on the floor. She sat very still and very quiet. She waited and waited.

Then two little eyes peeked out. The kitten took one small step. Then another. It came all the way out and sniffed Ella's shoe.

"Hello, kitten," Ella whispered. The kitten rubbed against her hand.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together.
story:
Ayla stood in the band room. Her drum sat on the floor. She patted it. Boom, boom, boom. Her friend Milo patted his drum too. Boomboomboom, so fast! Their sounds bumped into each other. It was a mess.

"Can we make it sound nice?" Ayla asked. "Yes, let's try my way," said Milo. Milo patted his knees. Pat, pat, pat. He went slow and even. Ayla watched him. Then she patted too. Pat, pat, pat. Their hands went up and down together, straight like a line. Boom, boom, boom. The drums sounded like one big drum!

Ayla unzipped the zipper on her drum bag. She put her drumsticks inside. "Tomorrow we play more?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Milo. They waved and walked out the door.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Other languages have their own words for thank you, like 'gracias' in Spanish.
story:
Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her plate was almost empty. She wanted more rice.

"Mama, may I have more rice, please?" she asked.

"Yes! What nice words," said Mama. She scooped the rice onto the plate.

Sienna slid her fork toward the rice. She took one bite. Then two bites. Then three bites. Yum.

Then her fork slipped. Clang! It fell on the floor.

"Sorry, Mama," said Sienna.

"That is okay," said Mama. She got a new fork.

"Papa, can you help me cut the chicken, please?" asked Sienna.

Papa cut it into little pieces. "There you go."

"Thank you," said Sienna.

Papa smiled big. "You know what my friend Marco says at the playground? He says gracias. That is his word for thank you."

"Gracias," said Sienna. She said it once. She said it twice. She said it three times.

"Grass-ee-ahs," she said slowly.

"Perfect!" said Papa.

Sienna looked at her empty plate. She held it up high.

"Gracias, Mama!"

Mama laughed and clapped. "One more little scoop for you."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We say "thank you" when someone gives us something or helps us.
story:
Camille sat at the dinner table. Grandma set down a bowl of peas. Then Grandma gave Camille a shiny red spoon. It was just for Camille. New and bright and hers.

Camille ate her peas fast. She wanted to try the corn too. "Can I have some corn?" she asked. Daddy scooped corn onto her plate. Camille dug in her spoon right away. Then she stopped. Wait. Grandma gave her the spoon. Daddy gave her the corn. Nobody had gotten a "thank you" yet.

Camille looked at the shiny spoon. What would happen if she said it? She took a big breath. "Thank you, Grandma, for my spoon." Grandma's face went all warm and smiley. "Thank you, Daddy, for the corn." Daddy smiled too, and gave Mommy the corn next, so it was fair.

Then Camille saw a little bug on the window. "Look!" she said. "A bug at dinner!" Mommy laughed. "He is smelly, maybe," said Camille, and everyone giggled. Daddy used a cup to carry the bug outside. Camille waved at the door. "Bye, bug," she said. "Thank you for visiting us."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
story:
Jaxson wanted to help in the kitchen. His grandma was making soup on the stove. The pot went bubble, bubble. Steam rose up from the pot. Grandma said, "Stay back, Jaxson. The pot is hot." Jaxson stayed close to her legs. He touched the cold fridge instead. It felt smooth and cool.

Grandma gave him a job. He could put spoons on the counter. He carried them one by one. His tummy felt happy. He was a good helper.

Then Jaxson saw something on the wall. It was a small hole with little slots. It was down low, near the floor. He put down his spoon. He did not touch the hole. He did not put his fingers in it. "Grandma, come look," he said. Grandma came right over. "Good boy," she said. "We never touch that. I will cover it up." She plugged in a safe cover. It clicked into place. Jaxson smiled and picked up his spoon again.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Now means at this very moment.
story:
Bennett woke up in his bedroom. The sun was up. "Is it today now?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Yesterday we went to the park. Today we stay home."

Bennett wanted a story. "Read now, please," he said. "Not now," said Mama. "The story is later, after breakfast." Bennett sighed. "Now means right this minute," he said to his teddy. "Later means not yet."

Bennett ate his eggs. He drank his milk. Then he pulled the round knob on his curtain. The curtain slid shut. The room went dark. He pulled it back open. The room went sunny again. He laughed. "Look, teddy! I close it, it is dark. I open it, it is light!"

"After breakfast is now," said Mama. "Story time!" Bennett jumped on his soft rug. He did not miss one page. Yesterday they had gone on the swing. Today was story day. Tomorrow, Mama said, they would swing again.

"When is tomorrow?" asked Bennett.

"Not today," said Mama. "Tomorrow comes after sleep."

Bennett hugged his teddy. "Story now," he whispered. "Swing tomorrow."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: The odd one out is the thing that does not belong in a group.
story:
Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. She was very hungry and a little thirsty too. Mama set out a big plate of apples, cheese and grapes. Next to the food, Rosalie saw her toy box was open. Her toy cars had rolled out onto the table!

"Look, Mama, look!" said Rosalie. She pointed at the cars. There was a red car, a blue car, a green car. And there, behind them, something yellow. It was long and curved. It was a banana!

"A banana does not belong with the cars," said Rosalie. She picked it up. It felt smooth and cool. It smelled sweet like a snack. The banana was the odd one out!

"Good spotting," said Mama. "That banana is a gift for you. Put it with the food."

Rosalie placed the banana with the apples and grapes. Now the cars were all cars. The food was all food. Everything was in its right group. Rosalie clapped her hands. "Dinner time!" she said, and took a big happy bite.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: You can keep the beat by tapping your knees, stamping your feet or tapping a drum.
story:
Jaxon was at his friend Mia's house. Mia had a little drum. She hit it. Boom, boom, boom. "It goes steady," said Jaxon. "Like walking feet."

Mia sang a song. "Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake." Jaxon clapped along. Clap, clap, clap. Then his hands got tired. They hurt a little bit. He stopped.

What could he do now? He looked down at his shoes. Could feet keep the beat too? Jaxon stamped the floor. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Yes! His feet went steady, just like the drum. Boom went the drum. Stomp went his feet. One, two, one, two.

Mia stamped too. They sang the song together. "Bake me a cake as fast as you can." Jaxon sang the words all by himself. He did not forget any. After the song, Mia drew a rainbow on paper. It had red, yellow and blue. "Sing it again," said Jaxon. He tapped his knees this time. Pat, pat, pat. The beat went on and on.
